title: Maintaining
hookLine: keeping good states going and growing

cards: Day one of a new habit has the thrill of starting. Day two is just doing it again. No fanfare, no new pen.
A beautiful journal gets three lovely pages, and six months later it turns up under the bed, the rest of it blank. Starting a good thing is the third effort.
Keeping it going is the fourth, and for this one the Buddha reached for pictures from the farmyard and the workshop.

teach.b: The fourth effort, in the Numbered Discourses, is for wholesome states already arisen: you work to keep them, so they don't fade or get muddled, and help them grow to fullness.
The Pali name is anurakkhaṇā, protecting, guarding what you have. The list's own example is a meditator protecting a steady object of concentration once they've found it.
But how do you keep at something without straining? A sutta in the Connected Discourses gives two pictures.
A hen sits on her eggs, eight or ten or twelve, covering them, warming them, tending them properly. She doesn't need to wish, may my chicks break out today. If she keeps sitting, they will.
Then a carpenter looks at the handle of his adze, a woodworking tool, and sees the marks his fingers have worn into it. He couldn't say how much wore away today, or yesterday. But it wore.
Just so, the Buddha says, a monk can't see how much of the mind's taints wore away today, but steady practice wears them away.

teach.h: DO IT AGAIN, AND ENJOY IT.
teach.b: The Dhammapada adds the other half, in Max Müller's words: "If a man does what is good, let him do it again; let him delight in it: happiness is the outcome of good."
Gladness isn't a distraction from keeping a good thing going. It's part of what keeps it going.

how: Buddhist practitioners keep daily routines, a morning sit, evening chanting, regular offerings, and many traditions encourage rejoicing in one's own good deeds as a way of sustaining them.

o: holding on tight so nothing ever changes
keeping good qualities going and growing

games.q: keeping it going: tap the pairs.
p: worn away, unseen day by day

s: the Buddha says you'll be able to see your progress each day
the carpenter can't tell how much of the handle wore away today, but it wears.
the Dhammapada says to repeat good deeds and delight in them
in Müller's words, 'let him do it again; let him delight in it'.
maintaining is only about not losing ground
the fourth effort also helps the good grow to fullness.

games.q: you're a hen with a clutch of eggs. by SN 22.101, what gets the chicks out?
games.why: the Buddha says a hen who covers and warms her eggs properly needn't wish for the chicks to hatch; they will. steady practice works the same way.

practice: Bring back any good thing you've been doing lately, without measuring it or asking whether it's working.
Picture yourself doing it again, the way a hen settles back onto her eggs, no fuss, no wishing, and let a little gladness come with the picture if it wants to.

wordCard.voice: Maintaining. Anurakkhaṇā, the fourth effort: keeping good states going and growing, like a hen sitting on her eggs.

orig.note: Pali anurakkhaṇā: protecting, guarding; the fourth right effort.

carryVoice: Your line: keep it going. The hen just keeps sitting, and in time the chicks break out. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Samyutta Nikaya 22.101 (Vasijata or Nava Sutta, the hen and the adze handle)
